examples.q: In 4x + 7, identify the variable and the constant term.
examples.misconception: Calling 4 a constant because it is a number; 4 is the coefficient attached to x.
examples.visual: Expression tiles labelled 4, x and 7; the 4 and x form one 4x term. Targets: variable-x, coefficient-four, constant-seven.
steps: Show the expression
Write 4x + 7 with 4 attached to x and 7 separate.
Read the whole expression first: one part depends on x and one part is fixed.
Identify what changes
Highlight x inside the 4x term; leave 4 and 7 unhighlighted.
The letter x can take different values, so x is the variable.
Identify what stays fixed
Highlight the separate +7 tile, then label variable x and constant 7.
Seven is added regardless of the value of x, so seven is the constant.
examples.verify: With x = 2 the expression is 15; with x = 3 it is 19. The 7 stays fixed.
examples.repair: Vary x while holding +7 fixed; ask which symbol changed and why 4 is attached to x.

examples.q: What is the coefficient of a in -3a + 5?
examples.misconception: Dropping the minus sign and reporting 3.
examples.visual: A signed term card -3a, partitioned into multiplier -3 and variable a, plus a separate +5 card. Targets: signed-term, coefficient-minus-three, variable-a.
steps: Isolate the term
Box -3a as one term, with its minus sign attached.
The sign belongs to this term; we cannot leave it behind.
Expose its factors
Separate -3 × a without changing its value.
The number multiplying a is negative three.
Name the coefficient
Label -3 and leave +5 outside the term box.
The coefficient of a is negative three, not positive three.
examples.verify: For a = 2, -3a = -6. Using +3 would produce +6 and fail.
examples.repair: Replace a with 1 and -1 to show that the multiplier remains -3; reselect the whole signed term.

examples.misconception: Listing 4y without its minus sign or treating x and y as separate terms.
examples.visual: A horizontal expression ribbon with boundaries before -4y and +9; each sign travels with its term. Targets: term-2x, term-minus-4y, term-9.
steps: Find operation boundaries
Place dividers at the subtraction and addition boundaries.
Terms are the pieces joined by addition or subtraction.
Carry each sign
Move the minus into the -4y card; retain +9 as a positive constant.
The middle term is negative four y, including its sign.
Count and list
Number the three intact cards in reading order.
There are three terms: two x, negative four y and nine.
examples.verify: Rejoining the three cards gives 2x + (-4y) + 9, the original expression.
examples.repair: Rebuild the expression from signed cards, then ask which card must carry the minus to preserve the original.

examples.q: Write an expression for five more than three times n.
examples.misconception: Writing 5n + 3 by translating words in reading order.
examples.visual: Three n tiles grouped as 3n; five unit tiles join afterwards. Targets: three-n-groups, plus-five, composed-expression.
steps: Make three times n
Duplicate the n tile into three equal copies and group them.
Three times n means three copies of the same unknown: three n.
Add five
Introduce five unit tiles to the right of the group.
Five more than that total means add five after the multiplication.
Write the expression
Replace the groups with 3n + 5; do not show an equals sign.
The expression is three n plus five.
examples.verify: For n = 2, three times two plus five is 11; 3n + 5 also gives 11.
states: three times n; five more, as words
three n tiles plus five unit tiles
examples.repair: Make three n groups before showing the five units; compare the incorrect 5n + 3 at n = 2.

examples.q: Write an expression for five less than three times n.
examples.visual: Start with three n tiles, then remove five units from a numeric offset lane; a comparison chip contrasts 3n - 5 and 5 - 3n. Targets: base-3n, remove-five, order-check.
steps: Set the reference amount
Construct the three n group before showing any subtraction.
Three times n is the amount we are reducing.
Reduce by five
Animate a -5 operation after that group.
Five less than an amount means subtract five from that amount.
Check order
At n = 4, display 12 - 5 = 7 alongside 5 - 12 = -7.
These expressions differ. The wording gives three n minus five.
examples.verify: At n = 4, the phrase is five below 12, namely 7; 3n - 5 = 7.
states: five less than three times n, as words
examples.repair: Anchor the starting amount at 3n, physically remove five, and test both subtraction orders at n = 4.

examples.q: Write an expression for half of p, increased by seven.
examples.misconception: Writing (p + 7)/2 and accidentally halving the seven as well.
examples.visual: Split a p length bar into two equal halves; add seven unit squares outside that divided bar. Targets: p-bar, half-p, outside-plus-seven.
steps: Halve p
Cut the p bar into two equal segments and select one.
Half of p is p divided by two.
Increase the half
Attach seven independent unit squares after the half bar.
We increase the half by seven; the seven is not inside the division.
Write and contrast
Show p/2 + 7, then briefly compare it with (p + 7)/2 at p = 10.
At p equals ten, the intended result is 12, while halving the whole sum gives 8.5.
examples.verify: For p = 10, half is 5 and five increased by seven is 12.
states: half of p, then seven, as words
examples.repair: Draw the division bar around p only, place +7 outside it, and compare the two candidate expressions at p = 10.

examples.q: For x = 3, evaluate 2x and x². Are they the same operation?
examples.visual: Two x bars of length 3 beside a 3-by-3 square grid. Targets: two-x-bars, square-three-by-three, values-six-nine.
steps: Model 2x
Display two separate bars of length three and count six cells.
Two x is two copies of x, which gives six when x is three.
Model x squared
Build a square with three rows and three columns.
x squared multiplies x by itself, giving nine when x is three.
Compare
Place 6 and 9 below their respective models, with distinct operation labels.
The answers differ because multiplication by two is not squaring.
examples.repair: Count two bars of length three separately from a three-by-three array; ask what each superscript means.

examples.misconception: Combining all three terms into 3x or 6x - 3x.
examples.visual: Four x tiles plus two x tiles and a separate negative-three counter lane. Targets: group-four-x, group-two-x, constant-minus-three, six-x.
steps: Classify terms
Colour both x groups together; place -3 in a separate constant lane.
Only the x groups are like terms here.
Join like groups
Move the two x tiles beside the four x tiles and recount six x tiles.
Four x plus two x equals six x.
Retain the constant
Carry the untouched -3 lane into the simplified result.
The negative three remains, so the expression is six x minus three.
examples.verify: At x = 2, the original is 8 + 4 - 3 = 9 and 6x - 3 is 12 - 3 = 9.
examples.repair: Sort x tiles and constant counters into different lanes; combine only objects in the same lane.

examples.q: A learner writes 2a + 3b = 5ab. Explain the error and give the correct simplified form.
examples.answer: a and b are unlike terms; 2a + 3b cannot be combined further.
examples.misconception: Adding coefficients while multiplying the variables.
examples.visual: Two a-length bars and three b-length bars with separate shape codes; a crossed invalid 5ab card appears only after learner inspection. Targets: a-group, b-group, invalid-card, unchanged-result.
steps: Represent each group
Show two a bars and three differently shaped b bars.
The groups measure different unknowns, so their counts cannot be joined as one kind of tile.
Locate the invalid move
Highlight the proposed arrow from 2a + 3b to 5ab.
Adding the coefficients does not create a product ab.
Preserve valid form
Keep the two groups separate and display 2a + 3b.
These are unlike terms; the original sum is already simplified.
examples.verify: At a = 1 and b = 2, the sum is 8 but 5ab is 10; they cannot be equivalent.
states: two a bars and three b bars
examples.repair: Use a = 1 and b = 2 to falsify 5ab, then retain the two unlike groups as a sum.

examples.q: For -2x², identify the coefficient, variable and exponent, then evaluate it at x = -3.
examples.misconception: Squaring the negative coefficient, or treating -2x² as (-2x)².
examples.visual: Expression tree with -2 outside an x-by-x area grid; -3 substitutes into both x factors. Targets: coefficient-negative-two, exponent-two, square-nine, product-negative-eighteen.
steps: Parse the structure
Target -2 as the outside multiplier and the superscript 2 on x.
The square belongs to x; negative two is a separate multiplier.
Substitute
Replace each x factor with -3, yielding -2 × (-3) × (-3).
Squaring negative three produces positive nine.
Finish multiplication
Group the two negative-three factors, then multiply -2 × 9.
The value is negative eighteen.
examples.repair: Place parentheses only around the substituted x, not around -2x; square -3 before multiplying by -2.

examples.q: A trip costs R12 per passenger plus one R8 booking fee. Write a cost expression for t passengers.
examples.misconception: Multiplying the one booking fee by the number of passengers.
examples.visual: A receipt model with t passenger rows each priced R12 and one fixed R8 footer. Targets: passenger-rows, per-person-twelve, one-booking-fee, total-cost.
steps: Count the repeated charge
Duplicate an R12 passenger row t times, then compress to 12t.
The passenger charge repeats once per passenger.
Add the once-off charge
Append exactly one R8 booking-fee row outside the repeated group.
The booking fee appears once for the entire trip.
Write the rule
Place the repeated and fixed costs in a single total.
The total cost in rand is twelve t plus eight.
examples.verify: For two passengers, the receipt is R12 + R12 + R8 = R32; the rule gives R32.
examples.repair: Show a two-passenger receipt with exactly one booking fee; ask whether the fee appears per passenger.

examples.q: Use C = 12t + 8 to find the cost for five passengers.
examples.misconception: Adding 12 and 8 before multiplying by five.
examples.visual: Five R12 receipt rows and a single R8 footer; the formula panel substitutes t = 5 beside the receipt. Targets: five-ticket-rows, product-sixty, fee-eight, total-sixty-eight.
steps: Substitute the count
Point from five passenger icons to t = 5 in C = 12t + 8.
Five replaces t because t counts passengers.
Calculate repeated cost
Accumulate five R12 rows to R60; display 12 × 5 = 60.
The repeated passenger cost is sixty rand.
Add the fixed fee
Join the one R8 footer to R60.
Sixty rand plus the booking fee of eight rand is sixty-eight rand.
examples.verify: Five charges of R12 total R60; adding exactly one R8 gives R68.
examples.repair: Count five R12 rows before appending one R8 row; compare R68 with the incorrect 5(12 + 8).

examples.q: A learner writes 2(x + 3) = 2x + 3. Find the first error and repair it.
examples.answer: The multiplier 2 must reach both terms: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6.
examples.misconception: Multiplying x but failing to multiply the 3.
examples.visual: Two separate complete (x + 3) groups; highlight the missing second set of three unit tiles in the learner claim. Targets: group-one, group-two, first-x, first-three, second-x, second-three, missing-three.
steps: Expand the physical groups
Show two full groups, each containing one x bar and three units.
The two outside the brackets counts two copies of everything inside.
Inspect the learner line
Match both x bars to 2x; match only one set of three to the learner’s +3.
The learner has not counted the three from the second group.
Repair and verify
Move both sets of three into a six-unit group, producing 2x + 6.
Two complete groups contain two x and six units, so the repaired expression is two x plus six.
examples.verify: At x = 4, left side 2(4 + 3) = 14; repaired right side 8 + 6 = 14, whereas 2x + 3 = 11.
states: two x bars and six units; missing three highlighted
examples.repair: Show the missing second set of three tiles in the learner model; repair the earliest wrong arrow.

examples.q: A rectangle has length x + 3 cm and width x cm. Write and simplify its perimeter.
examples.misconception: Adding only adjacent sides or doubling just the x part of x + 3.
examples.visual: A rectangle with all four sides separately labelled x + 3, x, x + 3, x; opposing side highlights precede term grouping. Targets: top, right, bottom, left, four-x, six-units.
steps: Label the full boundary
Reveal each of the four side labels in turn, including both copies of x + 3.
Perimeter measures the whole boundary, so we must count all four sides.
Write the sum
Trace the boundary and accumulate (x + 3) + x + (x + 3) + x.
The two lengths and two widths are all included.
Group like parts
Bring four x portions together and the two threes together.
Four x parts plus six centimetres gives four x plus six centimetres.
examples.verify: For x = 2 cm, sides are 5, 2, 5 and 2 cm; perimeter 14 cm, and 4(2) + 6 = 14 cm.
examples.repair: Trace and label all four sides before simplifying; count both copies of the +3 length extension.

examples.q: Are 3(n + 2) and 3n + 6 equivalent for every n? Explain and check at n = 4.
examples.answer: Yes. Both equal 3n + 6; at n = 4 both equal 18.
examples.misconception: Checking one value and claiming that alone proves equivalence for every n.
examples.visual: Three separate (n + 2) rows; regroup their n bars and six units without changing total; then a separate n = 4 check. Targets: row-one, row-two, row-three, three-n, six-units, substitution-check.
steps: Show every group
Create three rows, each with one n bar and two unit tiles.
The outside three means three identical copies of the entire bracket.
Rearrange without changing the total
Group the three n bars as 3n and all six units as +6.
Regrouping the same pieces shows the expressions match for any value of n.
Check a concrete value
Substitute n = 4 into both expressions and show 3(6) = 18 and 12 + 6 = 18.
The numeric check confirms our transformation at four, while the grouping explains why it holds in general.
examples.verify: For every n, 3(n + 2) = n + 2 + n + 2 + n + 2 = 3n + 6; at n = 4 both are 18.
states: three n bars plus six units
examples.repair: Regroup three complete bracket rows symbolically; use n = 4 only as a check, not the general proof.

practice: Identify the variable and constant term in 5m + 11.
The m part varies; 11 stays fixed.
Give the coefficient of q in -7q + 2.
Keep the minus with the q term.
A subtraction sign belongs to the following term.
Write four times k, increased by nine.
Form four copies of k, then add nine.
Write nine less than four times k.
Reduce the four-k amount by nine.
Write one third of r, then add four.
Divide r by three before adding four.
a and b are unlike terms; 4a + 2b stays as written.
At a=1,b=2, the sum is 8 while 6ab is 12.
State the coefficient and exponent in -5y³.
The minus belongs to the multiplier; 3 is on y.
A club charges R9 per entry plus one R15 registration fee. Write a rule for n entries.
Only the R9 repeats n times.
Four groups contain four copies of 2.
A rectangle has length a + 2 cm and width a cm. Find its perimeter.
Show 2(t + 5) and 2t + 10 are equivalent; check t = 3.
Both equal 2t + 10; both equal 16 at t=3.
Two groups each contain t and five units.
mastery: In -6z + 14, name the variable, signed coefficient and constant term.
1 mark for each correct identification.
Write an expression for eight less than half of p, then evaluate it at p = 20.
1 mark for p/2, 1 for -8 placement, 1 for value 2.
Simplify 7x - 2y - 3x + 5y, explaining which terms can be joined.
1 for grouping x, 1 for grouping y, 1 for 4x, 1 for 3y.
A learner claims 3(a + 4) = 3a + 4. Identify the first error, correct it and verify at a = 2.
3a + 12; both sides 18 when a = 2.
1 for first error, 1 for distributing to 4, 1 for corrected expression, 1 for numeric check.
A rectangle has length 2x + 1 cm and width x + 2 cm. Write and simplify its perimeter; check at x = 3 cm.
P = 6x + 6 cm; P = 24 cm at x = 3.
2 for all four sides, 2 for simplifying, 1 for substitution, 1 for unit and check.
parallel: After a signed-coefficient error: identify the coefficient in -9u² + 4.
Highlight the whole signed term before naming the multiplier.
After an operation-order error: write six less than twice v, then test v = 5.
Build twice v first, then subtract six.
After a distribution error: repair 5(w + 3) = 5w + 3; check w = 2.
Show five complete bracket groups, including all five threes.
practice_memos: In 5m + 11, m is the symbol allowed to vary. The 11 is a separate term unaffected by m; the 5 is attached to m as its coefficient.
Write the q term as (-7) × q. Its signed multiplier is -7. The separate +2 does not multiply q.
Read subtraction as addition of a negative term: 3a + (-2b) + (-6). The complete terms are 3a, -2b and -6; recombining them restores the question.
Four copies of k make k + k + k + k = 4k. “Increased by nine” adds nine afterwards, giving 4k + 9.
The base amount is four k, or 4k. Nine less than this is 4k - 9; at k = 5 the expression gives 20 - 9 = 11.
One third of r is r ÷ 3. The additional four sits outside the division: r/3 + 4; at r = 12 this gives 8.
Substitute x = 4 separately: 3x = 3 × 4 = 12, and x² = x × x = 4 × 4 = 16. These operations have different values.
Group the two p terms: 5p + 3p = 8p. Carry the unrelated -2 through, producing 8p - 2; at p = 1 both forms equal 6.
The a and b terms describe different unknowns, so 4a + 2b stays as a sum. At a = 1 and b = 2 it is 4 + 4 = 8, while 6ab = 12.
Separate the signed multiplier and the power: -5y³ means (-5) × y × y × y. The coefficient is -5 and the exponent on y is 3.
Each entry adds R9, producing R9n for n entries. Add the R15 registration fee once to obtain C = 9n + 15 rand; two entries would cost R33.
Replace n with 4 in the given rule: C = 9(4) + 15 = 36 + 15 = R51. The R15 charge appears only once.
Four copies of z + 2 contain four z terms and four copies of 2: 4(z + 2) = 4z + 8. At z = 3 both sides are 20; 4z + 2 would be 14.
The four sides are a + 2, a, a + 2 and a centimetres. Their sum is (a + 2) + a + (a + 2) + a = 4a + 4 cm.
Two full copies of t + 5 give t + 5 + t + 5 = 2t + 10 for every t. At t = 3 both forms equal 16; the rearrangement proves the general case.
